questions.question: What are the core AWS services a Java/Spring Boot developer should know, and what does each do?
questions.title: Core AWS Services Overview for Java Developers
questions.direct_answer: A Java/Spring Boot developer should be familiar with EC2 (virtual machines), S3 (object storage), RDS (managed relational databases), Lambda (serverless functions), SQS (message queues), and SNS (pub/sub notifications). Each solves a different infrastructure concern and maps directly to common backend patterns.

interviewer_intent.testing: Breadth of AWS knowledge and ability to map services to use cases
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing services without explaining when or why you would use them
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how services integrate — e.g., Lambda triggered by SQS, or Spring Boot reading from S3 on startup

sections.title: Why Service Integration Matters More Than Service Memorization
sections.content:
The trap in this question is treating it as a memorization exercise — listing 15 AWS services with one-line descriptions. Interviewers have heard that answer hundreds of times. What they actually want is evidence that you understand **how services compose** to solve backend problems.

A Spring Boot backend on AWS operates across three layers that mirror what you already do locally: **compute** (where the JVM runs), **data** (where state lives), and **integration** (how services communicate). Each layer has a default choice and an escalation path. The default is simpler and cheaper; the escalation handles specific requirements the default can't meet.

The connective pattern across all three layers is IAM — every AWS SDK call your Spring Boot app makes is authenticated via the task role or instance profile. Credentials rotate automatically without touching your code. Understanding this credential flow matters more than knowing what CloudFront does, because it determines how every service interaction actually works at runtime.

sections.title: The Service Map: Default vs Escalation for Each Backend Concern
sections.content:
| Backend Concern | Default Choice | Escalation Trigger | Escalation |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTTP microservice | **ECS Fargate** — containers without EC2 | Need event-driven, sub-second billing | **Lambda** (with SnapStart for Java) |
| Relational data | **RDS PostgreSQL** — managed, familiar JDBC | Need 5× throughput or global replication | **Aurora** |
| NoSQL / key-value | **DynamoDB** — single-digit ms at any scale | Need SQL flexibility, ad-hoc queries | Stay on RDS |
| Message queue | **SQS** — durable, pull-based, at-least-once | Need fan-out to multiple consumers | **SNS → SQS** pattern |
| Event routing | **SNS** — simple pub/sub | Need content-based routing, schema registry | **EventBridge** |
| File storage | **S3** — object storage, presigned URLs | Need block storage for EC2 | EBS |
| Caching | **ElastiCache Redis** — managed, VPC-native | Need global replication | ElastiCache Global Datastore |
| Secrets | **Secrets Manager** — auto-rotation, $0.40/secret/mo | Need cheap config storage (non-secret) | **Parameter Store** (free tier) |
| Monitoring | **CloudWatch** — metrics + logs + alarms | Need APM-level tracing | **X-Ray** or third-party |

sections.title: How Services Compose: The Patterns That Signal Real Experience
sections.content:
The interview differentiator is explaining **integration patterns**, not individual services. Here are the compositions that come up in real production architectures:

**SNS → SQS fanout**: A single order-created event publishes to an SNS topic. Three SQS queues subscribe — one for inventory, one for billing, one for email notifications. Each consumer processes independently at its own pace. If the billing service goes down, its SQS queue buffers messages until it recovers. This pattern decouples publishers from consumers and provides durability that SNS alone doesn't offer.

**Lambda triggered by SQS**: An SQS queue receives image-processing requests. Lambda polls the queue, scales automatically based on queue depth, and processes images in parallel. Spring Cloud Function makes the Lambda handler a plain `Function<SQSEvent, Void>` bean — your business logic stays portable between Lambda and ECS.

**S3 presigned URLs via Spring Boot**: Instead of routing file uploads through your Spring Boot server (consuming bandwidth and memory), generate a presigned PUT URL and return it to the client. The client uploads directly to S3. Your server only handles URL generation — milliseconds instead of minutes.

**ECS + Secrets Manager + RDS in a VPC**: The ECS task definition references Secrets Manager ARNs for the database password. The task role grants `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`. The ECS service and RDS instance share private subnets in the same VPC. No credentials in code, no public database endpoints, no manual secret rotation.

Spring Cloud AWS simplifies all of these: `@SqsListener` for SQS consumers, `S3Template` for object operations, and property source integration for Secrets Manager values as Spring properties.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ECS Fargate: containerized compute, no EC2 management** — push a Docker image, declare CPU/memory; AWS schedules placement; no AMI patching or capacity planning for the underlying host
- **RDS/Aurora for relational data; DynamoDB for key-value at scale** — Spring Data JPA works with both RDS and Aurora; DynamoDB requires the DynamoDB-enhanced client or Spring Data DynamoDB
- **S3 for object storage, not relational data** — cheapest durable blob storage; use for files, images, exports, and large payloads; not a database
- **SQS for point-to-point; SNS for fan-out** — SQS keeps messages until a consumer processes them; SNS broadcasts to all subscribers simultaneously; EventBridge adds content-based routing rules
- **Lambda for event-driven, infrequent work** — zero cost when idle; cold starts matter for latency-sensitive paths; use SnapStart or provisioned concurrency to eliminate cold starts for Java

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
AWS for Java backend work organizes around three layers — compute where the JVM runs, data storage, and the messaging and integration services that connect them. Knowing which service belongs in which layer makes it easy to pick the right one for each job.

**Compute — where the application runs**
- ECS Fargate runs Docker containers without managing EC2 instances — which means you define CPU and memory, push a container image, and AWS schedules and runs it; no patching, no capacity planning for VMs
- EC2 is the right choice when you need control over the instance type, GPU access, or specific AMIs; for most Spring Boot services, Fargate is simpler
- Lambda runs event-driven functions billed per invocation — which means zero cost when idle; the trade-off is cold starts and a 15-minute execution limit

**Data storage**
- RDS and Aurora handle relational workloads with full JDBC and Hibernate support; Aurora PostgreSQL adds auto-scaling storage and replicas with no operational overhead
- S3 stores object data — files, images, backups, large JSON payloads; not a database, but the cheapest and most durable way to store blobs
- DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL key-value store; useful when you need single-digit millisecond latency at any scale without managing schema migrations

**Messaging and integration**
- SQS decouples producer and consumer services with a durable queue — which means the producer doesn't need the consumer to be running at the same time
- SNS fans out one event to multiple subscribers — one publish, many consumers via HTTP, email, or SQS subscriptions
- EventBridge routes events from AWS services or custom sources to targets based on content-based rules

For a standard Spring Boot microservice: Fargate for compute, RDS for data, SQS for async communication — these three cover 80% of what backend services need on AWS.

questions.question: How do you set up a CI/CD pipeline for a Spring Boot application using AWS CodePipeline and CodeBuild?
questions.title: Deploying with AWS CodePipeline and CodeBuild
questions.direct_answer: CodePipeline orchestrates the pipeline stages (source → build → deploy). CodeBuild executes the build — it compiles the Java code, runs tests, builds the Docker image, and pushes it to ECR. The deploy stage updates the ECS service or Elastic Beanstalk environment with the new image. A buildspec.yml file in the repo controls what CodeBuild runs.

interviewer_intent.testing: CI/CD knowledge in an AWS-native context
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not caching Maven/Gradle dependencies in CodeBuild, leading to slow builds that download the internet every time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention CodeDeploy blue/green deployments for zero-downtime releases and integration with CodeGuru Reviewer for automated code review

sections.title: Why Dependency Caching Turns a 15-Minute Build Into a 3-Minute Build
sections.content:
A Spring Boot Maven build downloads hundreds of dependency JARs on first run — typically 200-500 MB. Without caching, CodeBuild downloads these on **every single build**, turning a 3-minute compile into a 15-minute ordeal. This is the most common CodeBuild mistake for Java projects, and the fix is a single `cache` directive in `buildspec.yml`.

CodePipeline orchestrates the end-to-end flow: **Source** (pull from GitHub/CodeCommit on push), **Build** (CodeBuild compiles, tests, and creates a Docker image), **Deploy** (CodeDeploy or ECS rolling update pushes the new image to production). Each stage is a separate concern — you can swap GitHub Actions for CodeBuild or replace CodeDeploy with Argo without changing the other stages.

The pipeline model enforces a disciplined workflow: every code change triggers an automated build, test, and deploy. The buildspec.yml file in your repository controls what CodeBuild runs, making the build process version-controlled alongside the code.

sections.title: The buildspec.yml: Compile, Test, Build Image, Push to ECR
sections.content:
The `buildspec.yml` is the heart of the CodeBuild stage. It defines the environment, commands for each phase, artifact output, and caching configuration. For a Spring Boot application targeting ECS Fargate, the build produces a Docker image pushed to ECR.

```yaml
version: 0.2

phases:
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - echo Logging into ECR...
      - aws ecr get-login-password --region $AWS_DEFAULT_REGION |
          docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $ECR_REGISTRY
  build:
    commands:
      - echo Building JAR...
      - mvn package -DskipTests=false  # tests run in the build
      - echo Building Docker image...
      - docker build -t $ECR_REGISTRY/$IMAGE_NAME:$CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION .
      - docker tag $ECR_REGISTRY/$IMAGE_NAME:$CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION
          $ECR_REGISTRY/$IMAGE_NAME:latest
  post_build:
    commands:
      - echo Pushing to ECR...
      - docker push $ECR_REGISTRY/$IMAGE_NAME:$CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION
      - docker push $ECR_REGISTRY/$IMAGE_NAME:latest
      - printf '{"ImageURI":"%s"}' $ECR_REGISTRY/$IMAGE_NAME:$CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION
          > imageDetail.json

artifacts:
  files:
    - imageDetail.json
    - appspec.yaml
    - taskdef.json

cache:
  paths:
    - '/root/.m2/**/*'  # caches Maven dependencies between builds
```

The `cache.paths` directive is what turns a 15-minute build into 3 minutes. CodeBuild stores the cached directory in S3 between builds. On subsequent runs, Maven finds all dependencies in the local cache and skips downloading.

The `CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION` is the git commit SHA, used as the image tag. This ties every container image to a specific commit, making rollbacks a matter of redeploying a previous tag.

sections.title: CodeDeploy Blue/Green: Zero-Downtime Releases for ECS
sections.content:
Rolling updates are the default for ECS — new tasks start, old tasks drain. But if the new version has a bug, it takes minutes to detect and more minutes to roll back. **Blue/green deployments via CodeDeploy** eliminate this risk: a completely new set of tasks starts alongside the existing ones, test traffic validates them, and production traffic shifts only after verification.

The deployment flow works like this: CodeDeploy creates a replacement task set (green) running the new image. The ALB routes test traffic to the green tasks on a separate listener. If smoke tests pass, CodeDeploy shifts production traffic from blue to green. If anything fails, it shifts traffic back — the blue tasks are still running.

The `appspec.yaml` in your repository defines the deployment hooks:

```yaml
version: 0.0
Resources:
  - TargetService:
      Type: AWS::ECS::Service
      Properties:
        TaskDefinition: <TASK_DEFINITION>
        LoadBalancerInfo:
          ContainerName: order-service
          ContainerPort: 8080
Hooks:
  - AfterAllowTestTraffic: "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123:function:smoke-test"
```

The `AfterAllowTestTraffic` hook runs a Lambda function that hits health and smoke test endpoints on the green tasks. Only if this Lambda returns success does CodeDeploy proceed to shift production traffic. The entire process is automated and auditable.

For teams that want even more safety, CodeDeploy supports traffic shifting strategies: **linear** (shift 10% every 10 minutes), **canary** (shift 10% first, wait, then shift 90%), or **all-at-once** (instant switch). For latency-sensitive services, canary with a 5-minute validation period is the safest approach.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pipeline = Source (GitHub) + Build (CodeBuild) + Deploy (ECS/CodeDeploy)** — each stage is independent; a stage failure stops the pipeline and the previous version remains deployed
- **`buildspec.yml` drives the CodeBuild execution** — define install, pre_build, build, and post_build phases; use environment variables for ECR URL, image tag (Git SHA), and ECS service identifiers
- **Tag images with Git commit SHA, not `latest`** — `latest` makes rollback impossible; committing the SHA as the image tag makes every deployed version traceable and rollback a matter of redeploying an earlier tag
- **CodeBuild service role needs least-privilege ECR + ECS permissions** — scope `ecr:PutImage` to the specific repository ARN; scope `ecs:UpdateService` to the specific service ARN
- **`imagedefinitions.json` connects build to ECS deploy** — the post_build phase writes `[{"name":"container-name","imageUri":"ecr-url:sha"}]`; the ECS deploy action reads it and updates the task definition

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
AWS CodePipeline orchestrates the CI/CD flow through stages — source, build, and deploy — while CodeBuild handles the actual compilation and packaging. Together they replace a self-managed Jenkins setup with managed infrastructure.

**Pipeline structure — source, build, deploy**
- Source stage: CodePipeline polls GitHub, CodeCommit, or S3 for changes; a push to the main branch triggers the pipeline automatically
- Build stage: CodeBuild pulls the source, runs the `buildspec.yml` commands (Maven or Gradle build, Docker build, ECR push), and stores artifacts in S3
- Deploy stage: CodePipeline invokes CodeDeploy or updates an ECS service, replacing old task definitions with the newly built image

**buildspec.yml — the CodeBuild instructions**
- `buildspec.yml` defines the phases: `install` (set up the JDK, Docker), `pre_build` (authenticate to ECR), `build` (run `mvn package`, `docker build`, `docker push`), `post_build` (update the ECS task definition image ARN)
- Use CodeBuild environment variables for the ECR repository URL, image tag (typically the Git commit SHA), and ECS service name — which means the build is reproducible and the deployed image is always traceable to a commit

**IAM permissions for CodeBuild**
- CodeBuild needs: `ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability`, `ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer`, `ecr:PutImage` for ECR; `s3:GetObject`, `s3:PutObject` for artifact bucket; `ecs:UpdateService`, `ecs:RegisterTaskDefinition` for deployment
- Use a dedicated CodeBuild service role with least-privilege policies; avoid broad permissions like `AdministratorAccess`

**Deployment to ECS**
- After pushing the image to ECR, the post_build phase generates an `imagedefinitions.json` file with the new image tag; CodePipeline's ECS deployment action reads this file and updates the ECS service to use the new task definition version

questions.question: How do you monitor a Spring Boot application with AWS CloudWatch metrics and alarms?
questions.title: CloudWatch Metrics and Alarms for Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot publishes metrics via Micrometer; the Micrometer CloudWatch registry pushes those metrics to CloudWatch. You then create CloudWatch Alarms on those metrics (e.g., high error rate, slow response time) that trigger SNS notifications or Auto Scaling actions. Application logs go to CloudWatch Logs via the awslogs Docker logging driver or the CloudWatch agent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Observability practices for production Java applications on AWS
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying only on infrastructure-level metrics (CPU, memory) without publishing application-level metrics like request latency, error rates, and business events
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Micrometer's dimensional metrics model, structured logging with logback and JSON format for CloudWatch Logs Insights querying, and composite alarms

sections.title: Why CPU Metrics Alone Can't Tell You Your Application Is Broken
sections.content:
ECS and EC2 automatically report infrastructure metrics to CloudWatch — CPU utilization, memory usage, network I/O. These metrics tell you whether the machine is stressed, but they can't tell you whether your **application** is healthy. A service returning 500 errors to every request uses almost no CPU. A service with a database connection leak shows normal memory until the connection pool is exhausted and every request starts timing out.

Application-level metrics — HTTP error rate, request latency percentiles, active database connections, queue depth, cache hit ratio — are what actually diagnose production problems. **Micrometer** is the bridge: Spring Boot Actuator collects these metrics automatically, and the Micrometer CloudWatch registry pushes them to CloudWatch as custom metrics.

The combination of custom metrics, structured logging to CloudWatch Logs, and CloudWatch Alarms creates a complete observability stack using only AWS services — no third-party tools required. The alarm triggers SNS, which notifies PagerDuty or triggers an Auto Scaling action.

sections.title: Micrometer Registry: Spring Boot Actuator Metrics → CloudWatch Custom Metrics
Structured Logging and CloudWatch Alarms: From Metrics to Actionable Alerts
sections.content:
**Structured JSON logging** makes CloudWatch Logs Insights queries possible. Instead of grepping plain text, you query `fields @timestamp, orderId, @message | filter level = 'ERROR'` across all tasks. Configure Logback to output JSON on ECS.

```xml
<!-- logback-spring.xml -->
<configuration>
  <appender name="STDOUT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
      <customFields>{"service":"order-service"}</customFields>
    </encoder>
  </appender>
  <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="STDOUT"/></root>
</configuration>
```

The ECS `awslogs` logging driver captures stdout and sends it to CloudWatch Logs automatically — no agent installation needed. Each task gets its own log stream within a log group.

**CloudWatch Alarms** turn metrics into actionable notifications. Create alarms on the metrics that matter for your specific service:

```bash
# Alert on high HTTP 5xx error rate
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "OrderService-HighErrorRate" \
  --namespace "OrderService" \
  --metric-name "http.server.requests.count" \
  --dimensions Name=status,Value=5xx \
  --statistic Sum \
  --period 300 \
  --threshold 50 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --evaluation-periods 2 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123:ops-alerts
```

The alarm evaluates every 5 minutes (`period: 300`), requires 2 consecutive breach periods (`evaluation-periods: 2`) to reduce false positives, and notifies an SNS topic that can page engineers via PagerDuty or trigger an Auto Scaling scale-out.

**Composite alarms** combine multiple conditions: "alert only if error rate is high AND latency is high" prevents alerting on a brief error spike that self-resolves. This is the difference between an alert that wakes someone up at 3 AM for a real incident versus one that fires every time a dependency has a brief hiccup.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`micrometer-registry-cloudwatch2` auto-publishes JVM + HTTP metrics** — add the dependency and namespace config; no CloudWatch SDK code; metrics appear in CloudWatch within 60 seconds of startup
- **Custom metrics with Counter and Timer** — `Counter.builder("orders.placed").register(registry)` for cumulative counts; `Timer.record(duration)` for latency distributions; tag with environment and service dimensions
- **CloudWatch Alarm on P99 latency and 5xx rate** — `HTTPServerRequests{outcome=SERVER_ERROR}` / total requests > 1% triggers alert; add SNS notification to PagerDuty or Slack webhook
- **Composite Alarms reduce alert noise** — combine CPU > 70% AND P99 > 500ms into one alarm; avoids alerting on transient CPU spikes that don't affect user experience
- **CloudWatch Logs Insights queries JSON structured logs** — `filter level = "ERROR" | stats count() by bin(5m)` correlates error spikes with metric alarms; requires structured (JSON) log output from Logback

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot's Micrometer integration publishes metrics to CloudWatch automatically — which means every service gets CPU, memory, HTTP latency, and JVM metrics in CloudWatch without writing any CloudWatch SDK code.

**Publishing metrics from Spring Boot**
- Add `micrometer-registry-cloudwatch2` to the dependencies and configure `management.metrics.export.cloudwatch.namespace` — Micrometer pushes all registered metrics to CloudWatch in the configured namespace every 60 seconds
- Spring Boot auto-configures JVM metrics (GC pauses, heap usage, thread count), HTTP request metrics (latency, count, error rate), and HikariCP pool metrics — these appear in CloudWatch without any custom code

**Custom metrics with Micrometer**
- `Counter.builder("orders.placed").register(meterRegistry).increment()` adds a custom counter; `Timer.builder("payment.processing").register(meterRegistry).record(duration)` records timing
- Tag metrics with dimensions like `service`, `env`, and `region` — which means CloudWatch dashboards can filter and group by service or environment without creating separate metric namespaces

**CloudWatch Alarms**
- Define alarms on metrics with thresholds: `HTTPServerRequests{status=5xx}` above 1% of total requests; `jvm.memory.used` above 80% of max; P99 latency above 500ms
- Alarms can trigger SNS notifications (which notifies PagerDuty or Slack via webhook), Auto Scaling policies (scale out when CPU > 70%), or Lambda functions for automated remediation

**CloudWatch Logs Insights**
- Spring Boot JSON logs shipped to CloudWatch Logs can be queried with Logs Insights — `fields @timestamp, level, message | filter level = "ERROR" | stats count() by bin(5m)` counts errors per 5-minute window, useful for correlating spikes in logs with metric alarms

steps: Adding the CloudWatch Micrometer registry exports all Actuator metrics — JVM heap, GC pauses, HTTP request latency, HikariCP connection pool, and cache stats — as CloudWatch custom metrics.
No code changes to your application; the registry pushes metrics on a configurable interval.

``xml <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId> <artifactId>micrometer-registry-cloudwatch2</artifactId> </dependency> ` `yaml management: metrics: export: cloudwatch: namespace: OrderService # custom namespace, not the default AWS/ECS step: 60s # push interval enabled: true tags: environment: production service: order-service ` The namespace is critical — it organizes your metrics separately from AWS infrastructure metrics.
The tags become CloudWatch dimensions, enabling filtering ("show me p99 latency for order-service in production").

questions.question: How do AWS Auto Scaling Groups work, and how do they benefit a Spring Boot deployment?
questions.title: Auto Scaling Groups — How They Work
questions.direct_answer: An Auto Scaling Group (ASG) maintains a fleet of EC2 instances or ECS tasks between a minimum and maximum count. It replaces unhealthy instances automatically and scales in/out based on CloudWatch metrics or scheduled actions. For Spring Boot on ECS, ECS Service Auto Scaling provides the same capability at the task level without managing EC2 directly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of horizontal scaling, health checks, and capacity management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Scaling too aggressively on CPU without considering JVM warm-up time — new instances may show high CPU briefly during JIT compilation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain scale-in protection to prevent terminating instances that are mid-request, and target tracking vs step scaling policies

sections.title: The JVM Warm-Up Trap That Causes Auto Scaling Storms
sections.content:
Auto Scaling sounds simple: CPU is high, add instances; CPU is low, remove them. For Java applications, this simplicity hides a dangerous feedback loop. A new JVM instance starts, the JIT compiler kicks in, CPU spikes to 90% during warm-up (class loading, JIT compilation, connection pool initialization), the scaling policy sees high CPU, launches **another** instance, which also spikes on warm-up, and suddenly you have 20 instances where you need 3.

This **scaling storm** happens because CPU-based scaling policies don't distinguish between productive CPU usage (handling requests) and initialization CPU usage (JIT compilation). The fix is twofold: set a **cooldown period** long enough for JVM warm-up to complete (2-5 minutes), and consider scaling on **request count per target** instead of CPU — a metric that reflects actual load, not startup overhead.

For Spring Boot on ECS Fargate, ECS Service Auto Scaling provides the same mechanics without managing EC2 instances. You scale the number of Fargate tasks, not the number of machines. But the JVM warm-up problem persists — a new Fargate task still runs a cold JVM.

sections.title: Target Tracking vs Step Scaling: Which Policy and When
sections.content:
**Target tracking** is the simpler and usually better policy. You specify a target value — "keep average CPU at 70%" — and AWS calculates how many instances are needed, when to scale out, and when to scale in. It handles the math and adjusts dynamically.

The advantage over manual threshold-based scaling: target tracking automatically adjusts for traffic patterns without you configuring separate scale-out and scale-in thresholds. The disadvantage: it reacts to the metric after it changes, not before.

```bash
aws application-autoscaling put-scaling-policy \
  --service-namespace ecs \
  --resource-id service/production/order-service \
  --scalable-dimension ecs:service:DesiredCount \
  --policy-name request-count-tracking \
  --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-scaling-policy-configuration \
    '{"TargetValue":500,"PredefinedMetricSpecification":{"PredefinedMetricType":"ALBRequestCountPerTarget"},"ScaleInCooldown":300,"ScaleOutCooldown":120}'
```

Notice the **asymmetric cooldowns**: scale-out cooldown is 120 seconds (respond to load quickly), scale-in cooldown is 300 seconds (don't remove capacity too aggressively after a spike). This prevents the oscillation pattern where scaling in triggers immediate scaling out.

**Step scaling** is useful when you need different responses at different thresholds — add 1 instance at 70% CPU, add 3 instances at 90% CPU. This handles sudden traffic spikes better than target tracking, which adjusts gradually.

**Scheduled scaling** handles predictable patterns: scale up before the morning traffic rush, scale down after business hours. For applications with known traffic patterns (e-commerce during sales events, B2B during business hours), scheduled scaling preemptively adds capacity before the load arrives, avoiding the response lag of reactive scaling.

For Java specifically, the metric that works best is **ALBRequestCountPerTarget** — it measures actual request load without being polluted by JVM warm-up CPU. Scale on real demand, not initialization overhead.

sections.title: Health Checks and Scale-In Protection: Preventing Service Disruption
sections.content:
Auto Scaling replaces instances that fail health checks. For Spring Boot, configure the ALB health check to hit `/actuator/health` with a response timeout that accounts for JVM startup. A Spring Boot app might take 30-60 seconds to start — if the health check interval is 15 seconds with an unhealthy threshold of 3, the ALB marks the task unhealthy before it's ready.

The right configuration: health check interval 30 seconds, unhealthy threshold 3, healthy threshold 2, and an ECS `startPeriod` of 60-90 seconds. The start period tells ECS to ignore health check failures during the initial grace period.

**Scale-in protection** prevents Auto Scaling from terminating an instance that's mid-request. Without it, a scale-in event during a long-running request (large file upload, complex report generation) terminates the instance and the request fails. ECS handles this with connection draining: when a task is marked for termination, the ALB stops sending new requests and waits for active connections to complete (default 5 minutes).

```bash
# Enable deregistration delay (connection draining) on the target group
aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes \
  --target-group-arn arn:aws:... \
  --attributes Key=deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds,Value=120
```

Set the draining timeout to match your longest expected request duration. For most Spring Boot APIs, 60-120 seconds is sufficient. For batch processing endpoints, set it higher or implement graceful shutdown in your application with Spring's `server.shutdown=graceful` configuration, which stops accepting new requests and completes in-flight ones before the JVM exits.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Target tracking scaling is the simplest policy** — set `CPUUtilization = 50%`; ASG adds or removes instances automatically to keep the metric near the target; no separate scale-in and scale-out rules to maintain
- **ELB health check enables self-healing** — ASG terminates instances that fail the ALB health check and replaces them; a JVM crash results in a new instance without manual intervention; configure the health check path and timeout to match startup time
- **Warm-up period prevents premature scale-in** — Spring Boot initialization takes seconds; without a warm-up period, a starting instance's CPU spike during ApplicationContext initialization triggers incorrect scaling decisions
- **Scheduled scaling for predictable patterns** — scale out before known peak hours; more reliable than reactive scaling for time-of-day patterns; combine with reactive scaling for unexpected spikes
- **ECS Auto Scaling operates at the task level** — Application Auto Scaling for ECS services targets task count, not EC2 instance count; use in combination with Fargate for fully managed scaling without ASG management

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Auto Scaling Groups maintain a fleet of EC2 instances or ECS tasks between a minimum and maximum count, replacing unhealthy instances and adjusting capacity in response to load — which means the fleet self-heals and grows or shrinks automatically.

**How scaling works**
- An ASG scales out (adds instances) when a CloudWatch metric crosses a threshold — CPU > 70%, request count per instance above a target — and scales in (removes instances) when load drops
- Target tracking scaling is the simplest policy: set a target metric value like `CPUUtilization = 50%` and the ASG adjusts the instance count to keep the metric near the target — you don't write scale-in/scale-out rules separately
- Scheduled scaling pre-warms capacity for known traffic patterns — add 20 instances at 8am on weekdays, remove them at 8pm — which is more reliable than reactive scaling for predictable load

**Health checks and self-healing**
- ASG performs EC2 health checks (is the instance running?) and optionally ELB health checks (is the application responding to HTTP health checks?)
- An instance that fails the health check is terminated and replaced automatically — which means a JVM crash or OOM that kills the process results in a new instance starting with no manual intervention
- Configure the ELB health check to call `/actuator/health` with a timeout that gives Spring Boot enough time to initialize before failing

**Warm-up period — the Spring Boot cold start problem**
- New EC2 instances need time to bootstrap the OS, start the JVM, and initialize Spring's ApplicationContext before serving traffic — configure the instance warm-up period to match your application's startup time
- Without a warm-up period, the ASG counts the new instance's metrics immediately, causing premature scale-in or misleading averages during startup

**ECS Auto Scaling** — ECS services have their own Application Auto Scaling separate from ASGs; the pattern is the same (target tracking on CPU or a custom metric) but operates at the task level, not the instance level.

questions.question: What are the VPC fundamentals a Java developer needs to understand when deploying to AWS?
questions.title: VPC Fundamentals for Java Developers (Subnets, Security Groups)
questions.direct_answer: A VPC is an isolated virtual network in AWS. Every production resource lives inside a VPC. Subnets divide the VPC into public (internet-accessible) and private (internal-only) zones. Security groups are stateful firewalls that control inbound and outbound traffic. Java developers need this to understand why their app can't reach the database, why Lambda can't call an external API, or why the ALB is unreachable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of network isolation and the security model that underlies all AWS deployments
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting RDS, ElastiCache, and application servers in public subnets to 'simplify' connectivity — this exposes them directly to the internet
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why Lambda functions in a VPC need a NAT Gateway to call external APIs, and mention VPC endpoints for private S3/DynamoDB access without internet traversal

sections.title: The Debugging Problem Every Java Developer Hits: 'Why Can't My App Connect?'
sections.content:
Most Java developers encounter VPC concepts not through architecture planning, but through a frustrating debugging session: the Spring Boot app can't reach the database, Lambda can't call an external payment API, or the health check endpoint returns connection refused. The root cause is almost always a VPC misconfiguration — a missing route, a blocked security group rule, or a Lambda function in a VPC without a NAT Gateway.

A VPC is an **isolated virtual network** that you define in AWS. It has an IP address range (CIDR block, e.g., `10.0.0.0/16`), and within it, you create **subnets** that divide the network into zones. The fundamental distinction is between **public subnets** (have a route to the Internet Gateway, resources get public IPs) and **private subnets** (no direct internet access, resources are internal-only).

The security model has two layers: **security groups** (stateful firewalls attached to individual resources — EC2, ECS tasks, RDS) and **network ACLs** (stateless firewalls at the subnet level). For most application deployments, security groups are the only layer you actively configure.

sections.title: The Standard Three-Tier Network Architecture
sections.content:
Production deployments follow a three-tier subnet model: **public** subnets for internet-facing resources (ALB, NAT Gateway), **private** subnets for application workloads (ECS tasks, EC2 instances, Lambda), and **isolated** subnets for data stores (RDS, ElastiCache) that should never have any internet path.

The ALB sits in public subnets across multiple AZs, receiving traffic from the internet. It forwards requests to ECS tasks running in private subnets. The tasks connect to RDS in isolated subnets. At no point is the database or application directly reachable from the internet.

The common mistake is putting everything in public subnets "to simplify connectivity." This works — until a security group misconfiguration or a misconfigured network ACL exposes your database directly to the internet. The three-tier model ensures that even a complete security group failure doesn't expose your data layer.

For outbound internet access from private subnets (pulling Docker images, calling external APIs, downloading packages), a **NAT Gateway** in the public subnet provides a one-way path: resources in private subnets can initiate connections to the internet, but nothing from the internet can initiate connections to them. NAT Gateways cost ~$32/month plus data processing charges.

sections.title: Security Groups: The Stateful Firewall That Controls Every Connection
sections.content:
A security group is a stateful firewall attached to a resource. "Stateful" means if you allow inbound traffic on port 8080, the response traffic is automatically allowed out — you don't need a separate outbound rule for response packets.

The key design principle: **reference security groups by group ID, not by IP**. Instead of allowing inbound traffic from `10.0.1.0/24` (which could include any resource in that subnet), allow traffic from `sg-alb` (the ALB's security group). This means only traffic originating from the ALB reaches your application — even if another resource in the same subnet is compromised.

```
Application SG (sg-app):
  Inbound: TCP 8080 from sg-alb         # only ALB can reach the app
  Outbound: TCP 5432 to sg-db           # app can reach database
  Outbound: TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0        # app can call external APIs

Database SG (sg-db):
  Inbound: TCP 5432 from sg-app         # only app can reach database
  Outbound: none needed (stateful)       # response traffic auto-allowed

ALB SG (sg-alb):
  Inbound: TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0       # internet can reach ALB
  Outbound: TCP 8080 to sg-app          # ALB can reach app
```

This security group chain ensures: internet → ALB → application → database. There's no path from the internet directly to the application or database, and no path from the database to the internet.

sections.title: VPC Endpoints and the Lambda-in-VPC Gotcha
sections.content:
When a Lambda function is configured to run inside a VPC (to access RDS or ElastiCache), it loses its default internet access. This surprises developers: their Lambda calls `https://api.stripe.com` and gets a connection timeout. The function is in a private subnet with no route to the internet.

The solution is either a **NAT Gateway** (adds ~$32/month and works for all external endpoints) or **VPC endpoints** for AWS services (free or low-cost, keeps traffic within the AWS network).

**Gateway endpoints** (free) are available for S3 and DynamoDB. They add a route to the VPC route table that sends traffic for these services directly to the AWS network without going through a NAT Gateway.

**Interface endpoints** ($7.20/month per AZ) create an ENI in your subnet for other AWS services — SQS, Secrets Manager, KMS, CloudWatch. Your application connects to the service via a private DNS name, and traffic never leaves the AWS network.

The practical benefit beyond cost savings: VPC endpoints eliminate the NAT Gateway as a bottleneck and single point of failure for AWS service calls. If your Spring Boot app makes heavy S3 or SQS calls, the NAT Gateway's bandwidth (up to 100 Gbps) and data processing charges ($0.045/GB) become significant. An S3 Gateway endpoint removes both the bottleneck and the cost.

For Lambda specifically, the cold-start penalty that VPC attachment used to cause (~10 seconds of ENI provisioning) was eliminated in 2019 with Hyperplane. VPC-attached Lambdas now have the same cold-start characteristics as non-VPC ones.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Public subnet: internet-accessible; private subnet: NAT outbound only; database subnet: VPC-internal only** — the three tiers isolate inbound exposure; ECS tasks in private subnets reach the internet outbound via NAT but cannot receive inbound connections
- **Security Group references instead of IP CIDRs** — ALB SG allows `0.0.0.0/0:443`; ECS SG allows only from ALB SG on 8080; RDS SG allows only from ECS SG on 5432; the chain locks access without maintaining IP allowlists
- **NAT Gateway enables private subnet outbound access** — ECS tasks in private subnets reach S3, DockerHub, and external APIs through NAT; NAT Gateway is charged per GB processed, which makes VPC Endpoints cost-effective for high-volume AWS service calls
- **VPC Endpoints eliminate NAT cost for AWS services** — S3 Gateway Endpoint is free; Interface Endpoints for ECR, Secrets Manager, and SSM reduce NAT data processing charges for services with high call volumes
- **Private subnet for all application components** — ALB in public subnet; ECS tasks in private subnet; RDS in database subnet (no internet route); this is the security baseline for all production Spring Boot deployments on AWS

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A VPC is an isolated virtual network in AWS where every production resource runs. Understanding the three-tier network model — public, private, and database subnets — explains why your ECS tasks can reach the internet but your RDS cannot be reached from it.

**Three-tier subnet model**
- Public subnets have a route to an Internet Gateway — resources in public subnets (ALB, NAT Gateway, bastion hosts) can receive inbound traffic from the internet and initiate outbound traffic directly
- Private subnets route outbound traffic through a NAT Gateway in the public subnet — which means ECS tasks can download dependencies, call external APIs, and connect to AWS services, but cannot receive inbound connections from the internet
- Database subnets have no route to the internet at all — RDS instances in database subnets are only reachable from resources within the VPC, which means a compromised external system cannot connect to your database even if it knows the endpoint

**Security Groups — stateful firewalls per resource**
- Every EC2 instance, RDS instance, and ECS task has a Security Group that acts as a stateful firewall — inbound rules specify what traffic is allowed in; outbound rules control what the resource can reach
- Use Security Group references instead of IP ranges — the ALB's Security Group allows traffic from any IP on port 443; the ECS task's Security Group allows traffic only from the ALB's Security Group on port 8080; which means the task is unreachable from anywhere except the ALB, regardless of what IP addresses are involved

**VPC Endpoints — private connectivity to AWS services**
- By default, calls from your VPC to AWS services (S3, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager) go through the public internet via the NAT Gateway — which costs money and adds latency
- VPC Endpoints create a private connection from your VPC directly to the AWS service over the AWS backbone — S3 Gateway Endpoints are free; Interface Endpoints for Secrets Manager, ECR, and SSM cost per hour but eliminate NAT charges for those services
